newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Serbs demand action on Moslem occupation of village.
newsitem.headline: Serbs demand action on Moslem occupation of village.

text.p: Bosnian Serb authorities accused NATO and U.N. police on Wednesday of failing to defuse tension over the Moslem re-occupation of a wrecked village on Serb territory, abandoned during the 43-month Bosnian war.

"Nothing has been agreed, they (NATO and the U.N. police) have not fulfilled their commitments to put the situation under control, return the Moslems and have them register regularly," the deputy police chief in Zvornik told Reuters by telephone.

"We will issue regular documents, identity cards, to every former inhabitant of the village who files for them regularly, and they can live there. They (the Moslems) came here illegally and unannounced. That is the essence of the problem," he said.
About 100 Moslems, some of them armed, entered Jusici, east of Tuzla, on Friday, just inside territory controlled by Bosnia's Serb republic.

Mostly destroyed in the war, the village sits in an area known as the "Zone of Separation", a demilitarised strip along the former front line which divided Serb forces from Moslem and Croat soldiers when fighting ended.

NATO, charged with enforcing the zone under the Dayton peace agreement, presented Bosnia's Moslem Prime Minister Hasan Muratovic in Sarajevo on Tuesday with some of the weapons which peacekeepers confiscated from the Moslems.
But the situation seemed no nearer resolution on Tuesday, with Serbs demanding the Moslems be removed, by force if necessary, and Muratovic trying to buy more time.
"We hope we can solve this without force," Muratovic told reporters.

The prime minister said that in future any Moslem trying to return to a village on Serb territory would follow a registration procedure agreed with the office of the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR).
But he said he had asked for time to get the new residents of Jusici the proper forms to fill out, making clear he hoped they would be allowed to remain in the village.
International representatives of the international community are trying to honour the Dayton-guaranteed right of refugees to return to homes from which they were driven.
They said this was being made more difficult by Moslem attempts to use the right of return to spark an incident.
"This was a clear attempt by the Moslems to provoke the Serbs. They went into the village with weapons, ready to fight," said a U.N. official who asked not to be named.
"It was a clumsy, silly move. Now they have been caught out and embarrassed. There is no way that this could have been successful and we're fortunate there hasn't been violence."

NATO sources on Monday told Reuters that Bosnian Serb authorities had set a deadline of Wednesday at 1500 GMT for the Moslems to depart. NATO spokesman Brett Boudreau on Tuesday denied any knowledge of deadlines.
U.N. spokesman Alexander Ivanko congratulated the Serb side for its calm response to the situation in Jusici.
"We believe under the current situation the (Bosnian Serb) Republika Srpska authorities deserve a pat on the back for their remarkable restraint shown in Jusici," Ivanko said in Sarajevo.
